card.hook: Nidaros Cathedral is so big that the best way to take it in is to step back and let it show off. It's the top-ranked spot on our Trondheim map, and one look at all that pointed, layered stonework tells you why.
card.stand_here: Stand near Vestfrontplassen, at the phone icon on the map, about 55 m west of the cathedral, and face east. From here the whole building fits in one frame without you pressing up against the walls.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole building. If it doesn't quite fit, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for towers, windows and carved stone details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the cathedral, and if the sky is bright, slide it a touch darker so the stone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening is a good bet, because the light is usually softer then. In the evening, switch on night mode and rest your phone against something solid to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the wooden Gamle Bybro (Old Town Bridge): use the front camera at 0.5x and face the Bakklandet side, so the cathedral rises above the trees behind you. Nobody has confirmed this exact angle, so check the view on your screen and shuffle until the cathedral sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand opposite the west front, by the row of benches, so the whole facade fits in the frame with you in it.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working place of worship, so be discreet when you take photos near visitors. It may also have ticketed areas or visiting restrictions, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take your big wide shot, then hunt for one carved detail in the stonework and see if a friend can guess where on the cathedral it is.
card.good_to_know: The cathedral stands over the burial place of King Olav II, who died in 1030 and became Norway's patron saint. Building began in 1070 and was substantially complete around 1300. A major restoration that began in 1869 was officially completed in 2001. It's the northernmost medieval cathedral in the world, it's still a working church that seats about 1,850 people, and Norwegian monarchs are still consecrated here.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Vestfrontplassen, at the phone icon on the map, about 55 m west of the cathedral, and face east. From here the whole building fits in one frame without you pressing up against the walls.

card.hook: Those heavy stone walls have probably been standing since the 13th century, and they look it. Every bump and seam is texture your photo will love.
card.stand_here: Stand near Erkebispegården, about 20 m south-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x for the long stretch of wall and the sense of scale. Switch to 1x for a natural view, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for windows, doorways and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line them up with the walls so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft light on an overcast day, or earlier or later in the day, usually flatters stone walls better than harsh midday sun. Go when it's quieter if you want clear views without people in them.
card.selfie_here: Head into the centre courtyard and turn so the palace buildings are behind you, then use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) to squeeze in the stone. In spring and summer the palace gardens are another lovely spot for a photo of you.
card.rules_and_safety: Parts of the complex are museums and used by the Church of Norway, so access may vary. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find one doorway or window set deep in the stone and frame it dead straight on the gridlines, then see if you can do the same with the cathedral just to the north.
card.good_to_know: The Archbishop's Palace was for centuries the seat and home of the Archbishop of Nidaros, and it's one of the largest medieval stone buildings in Scandinavia. After the Reformation it became royal property. Today it houses several museums, and the Regalia of Norway have been on permanent display here since 2006.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Erkebispegården, about 20 m south-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.

card.hook: Locals call this bridge the Gate of Happiness, and it's easy to see why. The bridge, the river and the old buildings on the banks all fit into one calm scene.
card.stand_here: Stand near Gamle Bybro, about 20 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face east and let the whole bridge fill the view.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to show the bridge as you see it. Switch to 0.5x for more river and bank buildings, and keep the bridge near the centre so the edges don't stretch. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it for details like the railings or the houses on the far bank.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the bridge up with a horizontal line so it looks straight, with a strip of water in front.
card.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset usually gives softer light and calmer water. After dark, night mode can work well if the river is lit, so rest your phone against a railing or wall to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Pose at one of the red wooden portals on the bridge, the 'Gate of Fortune', so it frames you. A visitor guide says many believe it brings good luck. Use the front camera, and check the framing on site.
card.ask_someone: Stand at the Bakklandet end of the bridge and ask a passer-by to shoot back toward the city centre.
card.rules_and_safety: Cyclists can pass the bridge at very high speeds, so watch for them while posing or taking photos on the crossing. Check the official site for works or closures before you go.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the rhythm of the railings leads the eye along the bridge, like you're about to walk across it.
card.good_to_know: The bridge was designed by Johan Caspar von Cicignon as part of the rebuilding after the great fire of 1681, and it was finished in 1685. It was first built of wood on three stone piers, with an iron gate in the middle that served as a guarded city gate until 1816. It was rebuilt in 1861 by the engineer Carl Adolf Dahl.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Gamle Bybro, about 20 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face east and let the whole bridge fill the view.

card.hook: Grass-topped ramparts, a pale stone tower and a whole city spread out below: Kristiansten Fortress practically sets up the photo for you. All you have to do is walk around and pick a side.
card.stand_here: Stand about 30 m north-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. That puts you on the grounds of Kristiansten Fortress with the tower ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the tower and ramparts together. Go to 0.5x for long wall lines, and try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the line of hills towards Byåsen.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines, with a wall or slope leading towards it. Then tap the brightest part of the sky and slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Pick a dry, clear day if you want the hills in the distance to show up. Early or late in the day, low sun gives the tower and walls more shape.
card.selfie_here: Try the Dronningens bastion (Queen's Bastion), on the ramparts of the southwest half-bastion facing out over the city. Use the front camera at 0.5x and check your screen to see the tower and the city fit in behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Place d'armes (the parade ground inside the fortress) and face north-west, with the donjon across the grass behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The road up to the fortress is very steep at the start, so take it slowly. Watch your footing near the edges of the ramparts. The grounds and the Donjon museum may have separate access arrangements, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the tower on a gridline, a wall leading to it and a perfectly level horizon, all in one shot. Bonus points if the sky behaves.
card.good_to_know: The fortress was built after the great city fire of 1681 and finished in 1685. It did its job in 1718, when Swedish forces besieged Trondheim and then withdrew. It was decommissioned in 1816, and the Donjon tower has been a museum since 1997.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 30 m north-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. That puts you on the grounds of Kristiansten Fortress with the tower ahead of you.

card.hook: Bakklandet is a whole neighbourhood of small wooden houses and narrow lanes, so don't hunt for one big view. Go for little scenes instead: a street leading the eye to the houses, a doorway, a wooden wall.
card.stand_here: Stand near Bakklandstorget, at the phone icon on the map, about 45 m south of the subject, and face north.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x in the narrow streets so you fit the houses on both sides. Zoom 1x works for most street scenes, and if your phone has 2x or 5x, use it for doors, windows and wooden walls.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the houses up with the vertical lines so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or later in the day is likely to be quieter, with softer light in the narrow streets. Daytime is fine too, but expect more people in your shots.
card.selfie_here: Try the Krana scenic lookout on Nedre Bakklandet, between street numbers 10 and 18, where the colourful wharves can sit behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low and out to the side so the wharves fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Old Town Bridge (Gamle Bybro) looking towards the Bakklandet side, while you stand on the bridge near its red arches so the wharves show behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: People live in these streets, so be considerate of residents. The lanes are narrow, so step aside when others pass and keep your phone close to you.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of a lane, then walk to the other end and look back. Can you spot how different the same street looks?
card.good_to_know: Bakklandet sits on the east bank of the Nidelva river, between the Bakke Bridge and the Old Town Bridge. In 1965 a road plan proposed knocking down a large part of it for a four-lane motorway. Local people opposed it, and by the early 1980s the plan had been shelved.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Bakklandstorget, at the phone icon on the map, about 45 m south of the subject, and face north.

card.hook: Here's a surprise: this royal palace is made of wood, it's pale and very long, and it just keeps going. Stiftsgården is more about sheer size than fancy detail, so your photo should show all of it.
card.stand_here: Stand in Stiftsgårdsparken, the garden behind the palace, and face west towards the building. Step back until you can fit the whole width of the façade in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole long front from the garden. Then try 1x for a tidier, less stretched view of part of the building, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the dormer windows and roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the roofline up with one of them so the palace sits nice and level.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, or on a bright but slightly overcast day, when the garden side is evenly lit and the colours are soft. Early morning or late afternoon light also works well for the garden.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie in the gardens in front of Stiftsgården, with the palace façade behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the same front garden, where the palace façade is in view, and photograph you with the building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine in the gardens, but interior photography is not permitted, so keep your camera for the outside. Check the official site before you go for palace opening, tours or garden closures.
card.challenge: Get one wide shot where the roofline is dead level and the lawn is empty of walkers, then one close-up of the dormer windows.
card.good_to_know: Stiftsgården was built between 1774 and 1778 for Cecilie Christine Schøller, a wealthy merchant's widow, and royalty and their guests have used it since 1800. With about 140 rooms and 4000 m², it is probably the largest wooden palace in Northern Europe. Much of the garden opened as a public park in 1906.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Stiftsgårdsparken, the garden behind the palace, and face west towards the building. Step back until you can fit the whole width of the façade in the frame.

card.hook: Picture a plain old grain warehouse wearing a glowing glass box on its head, like it's headed to a gig. After dark, that box lights up the whole street.
card.stand_here: Stand on Brattørkaia, on the opposite side of the street from the museum. Face across the road with the museum to the south-east, so you can see the whole building.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from across the street. If the building won't fit, tap 0.5x. To pick out just the glowing box on top, try 2x or higher, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the lit box, then slide the brightness down a little so the colours stay rich instead of washing out to white.
card.best_time: Go after dark, when the lights on the glass box are on. Daytime shots still work if you want the old warehouse walls, but the lights are much harder to see.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and hold your phone a little low and out to the side. Turn so the glowing building sits over your shoulder, and check it's in the frame before you tap.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the pavement and keep clear of traffic and any entrances while you take your photo. Check your surroundings before you step back to fit more in.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, keep the warehouse walls straight against them, and put the glowing box in the top part of your frame.
card.good_to_know: Rockheim is Norway's national museum of popular music, covering the 1950s to today. It opened in 2010 inside a grain warehouse built in 1919. The glass on top is printed with album covers and lit by 13,000 individually controllable LEDs, and visitors can even change the colours using their phones.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Brattørkaia, on the opposite side of the street from the museum. Face across the road with the museum to the south-east, so you can see the whole building.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with Rockheim behind the visitor, and none names a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole building in frame, so both fields are empty rather than guessed. The closest pages are general: Architravelguide (https://architravelguide.com/norway/trondheim/trondheim-photography-spots) and Europehighlight (https://europehighlight.com/norway/trondheim/photography-spots-in-trondheim-2026) describe the building's lit facade and roof at night but give no standing point. Roamee (https://roamee.xyz/guide/trondheim) and Cruise Alert (https://cruisealert.com/content/port-guide/trondheim-norway) place Rockheim near the Nedre Elvehavn waterfront, and Hotels.com (https://uk.hotels.com/de944293-st4/four-star-hotels-trondheim-norway/) mentions waterfront promenades with colourful buildings reflected in the water, but none of them says Rockheim is visible from there. No page I found states any selfie-stick or tripod rule for Rockheim or its surroundings, and none gives a safety point for these spots. A search with a named vantage point, such as a Nedre Elvehavn or Brattøra waterfront spot facing the building, could fill the gap.
